q: Cathode rays are fast moving electrons emitted from the cathode of a discharge tube.
e: True. Cathode rays are fast moving electrons emitted from the cathode of a discharge tube. Cathode rays are fast electrons leaving the cathode.

q: Cathode rays were discovered while studying the electric discharge through gases at high pressure.
e: False. Cathode rays showed up in a low-pressure discharge, not a high-pressure one. The written line says Cathode rays were discovered while studying the electric discharge through gases at high pressure.

q: Electric discharge first occurs at about 20 mm Hg.
e: True. Electric discharge first occurs at about 20 mm Hg. A glow discharge first appears near 20 mm Hg.

q: At very low pressure (~0.01 mm Hg), glass behind the negative electrode (cathode) is observed to glow.
e: False. The glow is on the glass behind the anode, the positive electrode, because cathode rays travel away from the cathode.

q: Cathode rays were first observed in 1869 by Julius Plucker and Johann Hittorf.
e: True. Cathode rays were first observed in 1869 by Julius Plucker and Johann Hittorf. Plucker and Hittorf first saw the rays in 1869.

q: Cathode rays were named in 1876 by Eugen Goldstein.
e: True. Cathode rays were named in 1876 by Eugen Goldstein. Goldstein named them cathode rays in 1876.

q: In 1897, British physicist Joseph John Thomson showed that cathode rays composed of a previously unknown positively charged particle.
e: False. Thomson showed cathode rays are negative. The particle was later named the electron.

q: Thomson measured the charge to mass ratio ($e/m$) of electron and found it to be $-1.759 \times 10^{11} \text{C kg}^{-1}$.
e: True. Thomson measured the charge to mass ratio (e/m) of electron and found it to be -1.759 × 10^11 C kg^-1. In 1897 J. J. Thomson showed the rays were a new negative particle, the electron.

q: The charge of the electron, $-1.602 \times 10^{-19} \text{C}$, was measured by Robert Andrews Millikan in 1906.
e: True. The charge of the electron, -1.602 × 10^-19 C, was measured by Robert Andrews Millikan in 1906. Millikan's oil-drop experiment measured the elementary charge e.

q: The mass of the electron is $9.107 \times 10^{-31} \text{kg}$.
e: True. The mass of the electron is 9.107 × 10^-31 kg. Keep the symbols and the sign in that relation.

q: Cathode rays travel in curved lines.
e: False. Cathode rays are electrons in a low-pressure tube. Thomson measured e/m. The written line says Cathode rays travel in curved lines.

q: Cathode rays have momentum and kinetic energy.
e: True. Cathode rays have momentum and kinetic energy. Kinetic energy is ½mv². It is the energy of motion.

q: Cathode rays cannot be deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
e: False. X-rays have no charge and cannot be deflected by both electric and magnetic fields. Cathode rays are electrons in a low-pressure tube. Thomson measured e/m.

q: Cathode rays can ionize the gases through which they pass.
e: True. Cathode rays can ionize the gases through which they pass. Cathode rays go in straight lines, bend in electric or magnetic fields, ionize gas, and make fluorescence.
True. Cathode rays can produce fluorescence. Cathode rays are electrons in a low-pressure tube. Thomson measured e/m.

q: The cathode ray tube (CRT) is a vacuum tube that contains an electron gun, a deflection system and a fluorescent screen.
e: True. The cathode ray tube (CRT) is a vacuum tube that contains an electron gun, a deflection system and a fluorescent screen. A CRT is a vacuum tube with an electron gun, deflection plates, and a fluorescent screen.

q: Before late 2000 AD, CRTs were widely used in cathode ray oscilloscopes (CROs), television sets and computer monitors.
e: True. Before late 2000 AD, CRTs were widely used in cathode ray oscilloscopes (CROs), television sets and computer monitors. Cathode rays are electrons in a low-pressure tube. Thomson measured e/m.

q: Flat-panel displays have higher power consumption than CRTs.
e: False. Work is F · s. Power is work per second, in watts. The written line says Flat-panel displays have higher power consumption than CRTs.

q: Cathode rays are visible to the naked eye.
e: False. Cathode rays are electrons in a low-pressure tube. Thomson measured e/m. The written line says Cathode rays are visible to the naked eye.
